lesson.title: How big, and will it replicate?

lead.text: Take the training course from the opening. In each class the scores are spread out, and nobody scores exactly the class average. Some do better than average and some do worse. The usual size of that scatter around the average is called the standard deviation. In class A it is about 3 points, so a typical student sits within a few points of the average. In class B it is about 30, so scores are all over the place.

The standard deviation matters because a gain only means something beside it. If scores wobble by 3 points anyway, a gain of 6 is a clear shift. If they wobble by 30, a gain of 6 is about what you would see between two groups of students who had no training at all. A change should be judged against the scatter in the scores.
Both classes gained 6 points on average from the course. Think about the scatter in each class.

That suggests a measure. Divide the gain by the standard deviation, and the answer says how many spreads the two groups have moved apart. In class A, 6 ÷ 3 = 2, which is two whole spreads. In class B, 6 ÷ 30 = 0.2, a fifth of a spread. This ratio is Cohen's d: the difference between two means (the averages) measured in standard deviations.

The figure draws each class's scores as a bell-shaped curve, one for the untrained group and one for the trained. Where d is 2 the two curves hardly overlap, and almost every trained student beats the typical untrained one. Where d is 0.2 the curves lie nearly on top of each other.

afterFigure.text: Because d counts in spreads, it lets you compare results measured in different units. Jacob Cohen suggested rough labels of 0.2 for small, 0.5 for medium and 0.8 for large, and warned that they are no substitute for knowing what counts as a worthwhile change in the field in question.

lead.text: A control group scores 100 on average and a training group scores 106. Scores in both groups scatter with a standard deviation of 15.

The d we have used so far assumed both groups scatter by the same amount. Often they do not, and one group may be tightly bunched while the other is loose. Dividing by the plain average of the two spreads would treat both groups as equally important, although the looser group says more about how unreliable the scores are.

The usual remedy is a pooled standard deviation. Square each group's standard deviation and average the two squares, then take the square root. Squaring makes a large spread count for far more than a small one, so the pooled value leans towards the looser group. When both spreads are equal the pooled value is just that spread, which gives a quick check on any working. Then divide the gap between the means by the pooled value, as before.

workedSteps.text: The standard deviations differ, so pool them. Square each one.
Average the two squares, then take the square root. This is the pooled standard deviation.
Divide the difference between the means by the pooled standard deviation.

steps.headline: The chance of finding a real effect

lead.text: Suppose the course really does help, with a true effect of d = 0.3. A study of a small group may still fail to show it, because a handful of students can easily be unlucky. Statistical power is the chance that a study detects an effect that is really there. A study with 80% power finds a real effect in 8 attempts out of 10.

Detecting needs a rule. A result counts as significant when, if there were no real effect, a gap this large would turn up by luck fewer than 5 times in 100. That 5% cut-off is written α = 0.05, and 80% power at α = 0.05 is the usual target.
Small studies have low power. They often miss real effects, and the few effects they do find tend to be lucky overestimates, because only an unusually big gap clears the cut-off in a small group.
A small study goes looking for a small effect, using a cut-off of α = 0.05.

steps.headline: How many people a study needs

lead.text: A study can be planned to have enough power. Lehr's rule of thumb gives the number of participants needed in each group for 80% power at α = 0.05: 16 ÷ d². For a large effect with d = 0.8, that is 16 ÷ 0.64 = 25 people per group.
Because d is squared, the number climbs quickly as the effect shrinks. At d = 0.5 the rule gives 16 ÷ 0.25 = 64 per group, and at d = 0.2 it gives 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400.

afterFigure.text: The two pictures show why. With d = 0.5 the curves are visibly apart. With d = 0.2 they overlap so much that it takes a crowd of participants to see the gap above the scatter.

lead.text: A team plans a study of an effect with d = 0.4. They want 80% power at α = 0.05.

steps.headline: A result that does not repeat

lead.text: A study finds an effect, and the next thing to ask is whether it holds up when someone else tries. A replication repeats the study with fresh participants. If the original effect was real, the repeat should find it again. If the original was a lucky draw from a small sample, the repeat will usually find less.

The Open Science Collaboration tested this by repeating 100 psychology studies. Of the 100 originals, 97 had been significant, but the repeats reached significance in only 35 of those 97 cases. Power posing, the idea that holding an expansive pose for two minutes raises testosterone, also failed to hold up when 200 people were tested.

Repeats carry most weight when they are large and preregistered, meaning the researchers published their plan, with the measures and the analysis, before collecting any data. They cannot then steer the result afterwards. A failed repeat of that kind counts for more than the original paper.
Ego depletion is the claim that self-control runs down like fuel. Published studies averaged about d = 0.6. A preregistered repeat across 23 laboratories tested 2,141 people.

lesson.orientation: Compute Cohen's d and the sample a study needs, then read failed replications as evidence.
lesson.reviewLabel: How big, and will it replicate?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A training course lifts test scores by 6 points on average. The organisers ran it in two classes. In class A, scores usually differ from the class average by about 3 points. In class B they differ by about 30. The single number 6 looks the same in both classes, and the organisers want to say how well the course worked.

The last lesson ended with a fair trial, which can show that a course made a difference. It cannot say whether the difference is big enough to matter, or whether anyone who repeated the study would find it again. Those questions run through this lesson.

We start with a way of measuring a gain against the ordinary scatter of scores. After that we look at how many people a study needs before a gain of a given size shows up reliably, and at what it means when a well-known result fails once other laboratories repeat it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll judge how big an effect is and how many people a study needs, and read a failed repeat as evidence.

recap.keyIdea: An effect is only as big as it is large next to the spread, which is what d measures. Small studies miss real effects and overstate lucky ones, so one result needs repeating.

blocks.text: Back with the training course, a 6-point gain gives d = 2 in class A and d = 0.2 in class B. You divided a 6-point gain by a spread of 15 to get d = 0.4, and found that an effect that size needs 100 people per group. A multi-laboratory repeat of ego depletion then gave d = 0.04, nowhere near the published 0.6.

recap.nextHook: So far the question has been whether a result is real, and the next lesson turns to measuring someone who must decide whether a faint signal is there, beginning with two guards who watch a car park.

questions.prompt: Two equal-sized groups have means 40 and 46.5 with standard deviations 7 and 17. Using the pooled SD √[(SD₁² + SD₂²)/2], what is Cohen's d?
hints: Square each standard deviation before averaging.
Average 49 and 289, then take the square root.
Divide the 6.5-point difference by the pooled SD.
questions.onCorrect: Pool the spreads from their squares, then divide the difference by that pooled SD.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the plain average of the two SDs. Pool the spreads through their squares.
That is the raw difference. Divide it by the pooled spread.

questions.prompt: Of 97 original studies with significant results, 35 replications were significant. What percentage replicated? Give one decimal place.
hints: Divide the successful replications by the studies attempted.
Use 97 as the denominator, since only significant originals count.
Convert 35/97 to a percentage and round to one decimal place.
questions.onCorrect: Only the 97 significant originals count. The replications that succeeded, over that base, give about a third.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count of studies that replicated. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the share that did not replicate. The question asks for the share that did.

questions.prompt: Which claim failed a large preregistered replication and should be treated as a cautionary case, not established fact?
hints: Two of the options are definitions or arithmetic; one is an empirical claim.

acceptedIdeas: Holding a power pose for two minutes raises testosterone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ranehill and colleagues (2015) found no hormonal effect of power poses in 200 people. The other two statements are mathematical facts.

choices.label: Holding a power pose for two minutes raises testosterone
Random assignment balances groups on average
Squaring r gives the shared variance

questions.onCorrect: Power posing's hormone effect failed a large replication. Arithmetic facts and balancing by chance are not claims that can fail that way.

misconceptions.feedback: Random assignment balancing groups on average is a property of chance, not a finding that was overturned.
Squaring r is arithmetic, so it cannot fail a replication.

questions.prompt: A course lifts scores by 6 points in two classes. Scores in class A usually differ from the class average by about 3 points, and in class B by about 30. In which class is the 6-point gain more impressive?
hints: Think about how easily a 6-point gain could be noise.
In which class would a 6-point change stand out from the usual variation?

acceptedIdeas: Class A, where scores vary little
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Class A: against a spread of about 3 points, a 6-point gain is large.

choices.label: Class B, where scores vary a lot
Class A, where scores vary little
Both are equally impressive, because the gain is the same size.

questions.onCorrect: A gain is measured against the scatter of scores. Beside a spread of 3, a gain of 6 stands out.

misconceptions.feedback: With a spread of about 30, a 6-point gain is lost in the ordinary variation.
The same raw gain means different things beside different spreads.

questions.prompt: A training course raises scores by 8 points, and scores spread with a standard deviation of 20. What is Cohen's d?
hints: d measures a difference in units of standard deviation.
Divide the difference between the means by the spread.
Divide 8 by 20.
questions.onCorrect: d is a gap between means counted in standard deviations: eight points against a spread of twenty.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference. d measures it against the spread.
That divides the spread by the difference. d divides the difference by the spread.

questions.prompt: A control group scores 100 on average and a training group 106, with a standard deviation of 15 in both. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Cohen's d is a difference measured in standard deviations.
Find the difference between the two means.
Divide that difference by 15.
questions.onCorrect: d is the difference between means measured in standard deviations: a gain of 6 beside a spread of 15.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference. Cohen's d measures it against the spread.
That divides the spread by the difference. d divides the difference by the spread.

questions.prompt: Why not simply average the two standard deviations?
hints: Which of the two groups has more spread, and which number should count for more?

acceptedIdeas: The pooled SD is built from the variances, so the group with more spread counts for more.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pooled SD is built from variances, so the more spread-out group counts for more.

choices.label: Standard deviations can never be averaged.
Squaring is needed only to make the numbers positive.
The pooled SD is built from the variances, so the group with more spread counts for more.

questions.onCorrect: Working from the squares lets the more spread-out group count for more, as it does in the data.

misconceptions.feedback: Averaging is allowed. The pooled value is simply a better combination here.
Standard deviations are already positive. Squaring serves another purpose.

questions.prompt: A small study chases a small effect. What is most likely?
hints: Think about how much noise a few people add.

acceptedIdeas: It will often miss the effect, and a lucky find will overstate it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With little power, a real small effect is often missed. Those found are usually overestimates.

choices.label: It will often miss the effect, and a lucky find will overstate it.
It will find the effect as often as a large study would.
It will always miss the effect.

questions.onCorrect: Low power means real effects are often missed, and the hits tend to be lucky overestimates.

misconceptions.feedback: Sample size drives power. A small study has much less of it.
A small study sometimes finds it. When it does, the estimate is usually too big.

questions.prompt: A team studies an effect of d = 0.4 and wants 80% power at α = 0.05. By Lehr's rule of thumb, how many participants per group do they need?
hints: Square the effect size first.
0.4 squared is 0.16.
Divide 16 by the squared effect size.
questions.onCorrect: The need grows with 1 ÷ d²: for this effect, 16 divided by the square of d.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by d. The rule divides by d squared.
That is the top of the fraction. Divide it by d squared.

questions.prompt: What is it called when a study is repeated with fresh participants to see whether its result holds?
hints: The word is in the headline of this screen.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replication: repeating a study with new participants.

questions.onCorrect: A replication repeats a study with fresh participants. One result is weak evidence until it has been repeated.

misconceptions.feedback: Reanalysis reuses the same data. This asks for repeating the study with new participants.

questions.prompt: A replication finds means of 50.4 (depleted) and 50.0 (control), both with standard deviation 10. What is Cohen's d?
hints: Divide the difference between means by the standard deviation.
The difference between the means is under one point.
Divide 0.4 by 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d = (50.4 − 50.0)/10 = 0.04, close to zero and far below the published average of about 0.6.

questions.onCorrect: The means differ by well under a tenth of a standard deviation, so the published effect did not hold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw difference in points. Divide it by the standard deviation.
That divides the SD by the difference. d divides the difference by the SD.
